meta.title: A parcel, doorstep to doorstep
meta.description: One 2.4 kg parcel followed from a front door in Bristol to a front door in Osaka: forty-two hours, nine handovers, two nested facilities and one scuffed label. The top level is the journey; the regional hub, its tilt-tray sorter and the border post each open into a scene of their own.
Everything up to the aircraft door. Domestic collection, depot sortation and night trunking into the regional hub.
meta.notes: Carriers call this the first mile. It is the least automated part of the journey and the part most often blamed for delay.

meta.description: The sorting hub and the airside cargo shed share a site so a parcel can move between them without a public road.
A notional boundary, not a place. While the parcel is airborne it belongs to no country's network and no scan can be added to it.
meta.notes: Drawn dashed because nothing here is a building — it is eleven hours of nothing happening.

meta.description: The tracking platform. Every scanner in every facility publishes to it, and it is the only thing the sender and recipient ever see.
Arrival, border clearance and the final mile. The parcel is handed to a partner carrier here — the sender's carrier has no vans in Japan.
meta.notes: Read this row right to left: the parcel lands on the right and walks back to a doorstep on the left.

meta.description: A flat in Bristol. The parcel is booked online, the label printed at home and taped to the box.
meta.notes: The label carries three separate things: a human address, a carrier routing barcode, and a customs data set.

meta.description: A driver working a fixed round of roughly forty collections between 14:00 and 18:00.
meta.notes: The van is a moving buffer. Nothing it picks up is sorted until it gets back to the depot.

meta.description: A spoke. Sorts the evening's collections into cages by destination hub, then loads them onto a trunk trailer.
meta.notes: A depot never sorts to a final address — only to the next facility. That is the whole idea of hub-and-spoke.

meta.description: A double-deck curtainsider running the depot-to-hub leg overnight.
meta.notes: Trunk departure times are the hardest constraint in the network. Miss the trailer and the parcel loses a full day.

meta.description: The one place every parcel in the region passes through. Opens into a scene of its own.
meta.notes: Runs a single six-hour night shift. Empty at noon, 11,000 parcels an hour at 01:00.

meta.description: Where trailers are emptied. Unloading is still done by hand — nobody has beaten a person at pulling irregular boxes off a stacked deck.
Anything the sorter cannot carry: over 31.5 kg, longer than 1.5 m, round, or unable to sit flat on a tray.
Belt, gantry and sorter. From the moment a parcel is singulated to the moment it drops down a chute is about forty seconds.
Chutes feed bays; bays are cage-built and sealed against a departure time, not against a parcel count.
Everything the sorter could not resolve. Between one and three parcels in a hundred end up here, almost all of them for a bad read rather than a bad address.
Twenty-two trailer bays. Trailers are called onto a dock in departure-time order, not arrival order.
Two people and an extendable boom conveyor that reaches into the trailer.
meta.notes: A good pair clears a double-deck trailer in about fifty minutes.

meta.description: Manual handling for anything outside the sorter's envelope. Scanned with a handheld and trolleyed straight to its outbound bay.
meta.notes: Oversize is a tiny share of volume and a large share of injuries and delay.

meta.description: Singulates the flow: takes a shoulder-to-shoulder mass of boxes and turns it into one parcel at a time with a fixed gap between each.
meta.notes: Singulation is the real bottleneck of a hub. The sorter can always go faster than the induction can feed it.

meta.description: An arch of cameras reading every visible face of the parcel as it passes underneath at 2 m/s.
meta.notes: Reads the routing barcode, not the address. The address was resolved to a sortcode when the label was bought.

meta.description: Takes a continuous scan feed off every reader in the building and publishes it to the tracking platform.
meta.notes: This feed is also the shift's live throughput number on the wall board.

meta.description: A 220 m closed loop of trays circulating at 2.2 m/s. Opens into a scene of its own.
meta.notes: Rated at 12,000 parcels an hour. In practice the induction lines hold it to about 11,400.

meta.description: Everything between joining the loop and being tipped: gap control, reading, weighing and the chute decision.
The two things a tray can do: tip left into a destination chute, or stay on the loop until the reject chute comes round.
Times each parcel onto a free tray. Too early and it straddles two trays; too late and the tray goes round empty.
meta.notes: The tolerance is about 40 milliseconds.

meta.description: Six cameras — four sides, top, and one shooting up through a gap in the trays — so the label can face any way.
meta.notes: Even with six faces covered, one to three parcels in a hundred come back as a no-read.

meta.description: Weighs the tray in motion and subtracts the known tare. Accurate to about 20 g at full speed.
meta.notes: Compared against the weight declared at booking. A large mismatch raises a revenue query, not a stoppage.

meta.description: Turns a sortcode into a chute number, checks the chute is not backed up, and writes the tip command to the tray's controller.
meta.notes: If the assigned chute is full it will recirculate the parcel rather than jam the chute.

meta.description: One of 1,100 trays on the loop. Tips 35° left or right on command and rights itself a metre later.
meta.notes: Every tray is addressable. The loop is effectively a moving array with an index.

meta.description: The lip of the destination chute. A parcel slides two metres down a steel slide into the chute below.
The default destination for anything with no valid chute. Deliberately placed last on the loop so it only catches what nothing else claimed.
meta.notes: A rising reject rate is the first sign a printer somewhere is producing bad labels.

meta.description: One chute per outbound destination — 188 of them around the loop. A chute holds about ninety parcels before it backs up.
Chutes are emptied into roll cages, cages are sealed and tagged, and the trailer leaves on its clock whether it is full or not.
meta.notes: A cage seal number is the unit of custody from here to the aircraft.

meta.description: A short belt under the reject chute feeding two manual encoding desks.
A person reads the label, keys the tracking number, and the parcel goes back to the induction line for a second pass.
meta.notes: About twenty seconds of work, but the parcel waits its turn in a queue that can run to twenty minutes at peak.

meta.description: The cargo shed. Cages are broken down and rebuilt into aircraft containers against a load plan.
meta.notes: Cut-off for a long-haul freighter is typically six hours before departure, not one.

meta.description: A widebody freighter running the sector nightly. Eleven hours in the air, no scans, no visibility.
meta.notes: The longest single event in the whole journey and the one nobody can shorten.

meta.description: Containers are unloaded and broken down, but nothing leaves the airport perimeter until the border releases it.
The import border post. Opens into a scene of its own.
meta.notes: Legally the parcel is not in the country yet. It is in a bonded area, which is treated as outside the customs territory.

meta.description: Paperwork first, goods second. Almost every decision the border makes is made on data lodged before the aircraft landed.
Non-intrusive inspection. An operator sees a density image, not a list of contents.
Cleared on the data alone. Nine parcels in ten never stop moving.
Held, opened and examined. Two to three per cent of parcels, chosen by the risk engine rather than at random.
meta.notes: Storage in the hold area is chargeable to the importer after the first free day.

meta.description: The single gate every route converges on. Until it fires, the parcel cannot legally leave the bonded area.
The national customs computer. The carrier lodges an electronic declaration against the flight manifest, usually before wheels-up.
meta.notes: Pre-lodgement is why most parcels clear in minutes rather than days.

meta.description: Matches the declaration to the airway bill: commodity code, declared value, origin, consignee.
meta.notes: A wrong commodity code is the most common reason a low-value parcel gets stuck.

meta.description: Scores every declaration against commodity, route, consignor history and value. The score picks the channel.
meta.notes: Scoring runs on the data, not the box. It has already decided the channel while the parcel is still airborne.

meta.description: Dual-energy scanner. Colours the image by material density so organics, metals and electronics look different.
meta.notes: Scanning is fast and cheap; it exists to keep the number of boxes actually opened low.

meta.description: Applies the tariff for the commodity code and adds import consumption tax on the value plus freight plus insurance.
meta.notes: Duty is charged on the landed cost, not the sale price — freight is part of the taxable base.

meta.description: A caged bonded store. The parcel waits here for an officer, not for a machine.
meta.notes: Nothing in this cage has entered the country. It can be re-exported from here without ever clearing.

meta.description: An officer opens the box, checks the goods against the declaration, and reseals it with tamper tape.
meta.notes: The examination is recorded against the entry, so the same consignor is scored differently next time.

meta.description: The entry is cleared and the bond lifted. Only now is the parcel legally in the country and free to move.
meta.notes: Release is a status change in a database. The physical parcel may not move for hours afterwards.

meta.description: The partner carrier's national hub. The parcel is now on a domestic label and a domestic sortcode.
meta.notes: The handover between carriers is a data handover as much as a physical one — two tracking numbers, one parcel.

meta.description: The last building. Parcels are sorted into rounds overnight and staged by van bay before the drivers arrive.
meta.notes: Sorting to a round is different from sorting to an address: the sequence within the round is decided later.

meta.description: A driver with 96 stops and a route the handheld re-sequences as the day goes on.
meta.notes: The final mile is roughly half the cost of the whole journey and the only leg the customer ever sees.

meta.description: An apartment in Osaka. The doorstep scan closes the tracking record and stops the clock.
Every scanner in every facility publishes to it. It is the only part of the network the sender and recipient ever interact with.
meta.notes: Tracking is a stream of events, not a location. Between two scans the platform genuinely does not know where the parcel is.

steps.name: Overview
steps.title: Doorstep to doorstep, 42 hours
steps.description: One parcel, Bristol to Osaka. Nine handovers across two countries, three of which are whole facilities in their own right: the regional sorting hub, the tilt-tray sorter inside it, and the border post at the far end. Nothing about this journey is unusual — it is what happens to a few million boxes a night.

steps.name: Label printed
steps.title: The label is bought before the parcel moves
steps.description: Booking online resolves the destination address to a sortcode and mints a tracking number. From this point the network routes on the barcode; the printed address is only there for the human at the end.

footer.text: The customs data set is captured **here**, at booking — not at the border.

steps.name: Collection scan
steps.title: The van arrives and the clock starts
steps.description: The driver scans the barcode on the doorstep. That first scan is what makes the parcel exist to the network — until then the booking is just a row in a database with no box attached to it.

steps.name: Round tipped out
steps.title: The van finishes its round
steps.description: The parcel now sits in a van doing another 39 collections before it goes anywhere useful. A collection van is a moving buffer: nothing on board is sorted, and the last pickup of the day travels the same distance as the first.

footer.text: **40 stops, 212 parcels** — our box is one of them and gets no special treatment.

waterfall.label: 2 h 24 m — rest of the round

steps.name: Depot sortation
steps.title: The depot sorts to the next building, not the address
steps.description: A spoke depot has no idea how to reach Osaka. It only knows which hub the sortcode belongs to, so it drops the parcel into a cage labelled with a hub, not a country. Every hop in a hub-and-spoke network is a decision about the next facility and nothing further.

steps.name: Tracking feed
steps.title: Every scanner publishes, continuously
steps.description: The depot's handhelds and belt scanners hold an open connection to the tracking platform and push events as they happen. What a customer reads as a location is really a stream of scan records — between two of them, nobody knows where the box is.

footer.text: Tracking is an *event log*, not a position. Long gaps mean no scanners, not a lost parcel.

steps.name: Cages loaded
steps.title: Cages go onto the trunk trailer
steps.description: Nine sealed cages for the same hub are wheeled onto a double-deck trailer. The seal number is the unit of custody from here on — the network stops tracking individual parcels and starts tracking the container they are in.

steps.name: Night trunk
steps.title: The overnight leg to the hub
steps.description: Trunking runs at night because the hub only runs at night. Every parcel in the region has to be in the same building at the same time for a single sort to work, and that window is roughly 22:00 to 04:00.

footer.text: Miss the trunk departure and the parcel loses a **full 24 hours** — the next one is tomorrow night.

steps.name: Trailer docks
steps.title: Inside the hub: the trailer is called on
steps.description: Trailers are not unloaded in the order they arrive. They are called onto a dock in the order their contents need to depart, so a trailer whose parcels all leave at 02:00 waits behind one that feeds a 00:45 departure.

steps.name: Oversize pulled
steps.title: Anything the sorter cannot carry comes off first
steps.description: Over 31.5 kg, longer than 1.5 m, round, or unable to sit flat on a tray — that goes down the oversize lane and is handled by people the whole way. It is a small share of volume and a large share of the injuries and the delay.

footer.text: **Not our parcel** — at 40 × 30 × 12 cm it is comfortably inside the sorter envelope.

steps.name: Onto the belt
steps.title: A boom conveyor reaches into the trailer
steps.description: An extendable conveyor runs right up to the trailer wall so the unloaders never carry a box more than a metre. The belt runs continuously from the moment the trailer is opened until it is empty.

steps.name: Singulation
steps.title: A mass of boxes becomes a single file
steps.description: Singulation is the real bottleneck of any hub. Taking a shoulder-to-shoulder mass of parcels and turning it into one box at a time with a fixed gap between each is harder than sorting them, and the sorter can always go faster than the induction can feed it.

footer.text: The sorter is rated **12,000 parcels/hour**; induction holds the real number to about **11,400**.

steps.name: Scan telemetry
steps.title: The gantry feeds hub control continuously
steps.description: The reader arch holds an open connection to hub control, which forwards every read to the tracking platform and puts the running throughput on the wall board. It is the same feed that tells a manager, at 01:30, that the reject rate has doubled.

footer.text: A rising no-read rate is almost always **one bad label printer**, not the readers.

steps.name: Into the sorter
steps.title: The belt hands over to the loop
steps.description: Past the gantry the parcel leaves flat belt and joins a 220 m closed loop of tilt trays circulating at 2.2 m/s. Everything from here is timed to the tray, not to the belt.

steps.name: Gap control
steps.title: Inside the sorter: timed onto a free tray
steps.description: The gap controller decides which of the 1,100 trays this parcel lands on. Too early and it straddles two trays and jams the discharge; too late and a tray goes round empty. The tolerance is about forty milliseconds.

steps.name: Six-sided read
steps.title: Six cameras, and still a no-read
steps.description: Four sides, the top, and one camera shooting up through the gap between trays, so the label can face any direction. Even so, one to three parcels in a hundred come back unreadable — and a taped-over, rain-scuffed home-printed label is exactly the kind that fails.

footer.text: **No-read rate: 1–3%.** At 11,400 parcels an hour that is up to 340 an hour needing a human.

steps.name: Weigh and cube
steps.title: Weighed in motion regardless
steps.description: The weigh cell weighs the moving tray and subtracts its known tare, accurate to about 20 g at full speed. Chargeable weight is the greater of actual weight and volumetric weight — length × width × height ÷ 5000 — which is why a big light box costs the same as a small heavy one.

steps.name: No chute
steps.title: No barcode, no chute
steps.description: The selector's whole job is turning a sortcode into a chute number. With no readable barcode there is no sortcode, so there is nothing to look up — it cannot guess from the weight, and it will not hold the tray while somebody works it out.

footer.text: The sorter never stops for one parcel. **Unresolvable means rejected**, not paused.

steps.name: Tipped to reject
steps.title: The tray carries it to the reject chute
steps.description: The reject chute is deliberately the last one on the loop, so it only catches what no other chute claimed. The tray tips 35°, the parcel slides out, and the tray rights itself a metre later ready for the next induction.

steps.name: The other 11,000
steps.title: What should have happened
steps.description: For everything with a readable label the tray tips the other way, onto a steel slide two metres down into the destination chute. That is the entire sorter for 99% of parcels: forty seconds from induction to chute, no human involved at any point.

footer.text: **11,400 parcels an hour** go this way. The bar beside this step is four minutes of normal running.

steps.name: Down the reject line
steps.title: Back out in the hub: the reject line
steps.description: A short belt under the reject chute carries the parcel to two manual encoding desks. Everything on this belt is here for a bad read, a torn label or a chute that was backed up — almost never for a bad address.

footer.text: **41 parcels queued** at the desks. Our box has just joined the back of it.

steps.name: Manual encode
steps.title: A person reads what the cameras could not
steps.description: Twenty seconds of work: read the tracking number off the label, key it in, and the system prints and applies a fresh machine-readable barcode. The work is trivial; the queue in front of it is not.

footer.text: **21 minutes waiting, 20 seconds of work.** Reject handling is queueing, not labour.

steps.name: Recirculated
steps.title: Back to the start of the line
steps.description: There is no shortcut back onto the loop — a recirculated parcel rejoins at induction and goes through the whole sequence again. Recovery is real, but it costs a second full pass and it is why a single scuffed label can cost half an hour.

footer.text: Recovered — and still inside the trunk cut-off, with **47 minutes** to spare.

steps.name: Clean read
steps.title: Second pass, clean read
steps.description: The fresh label reads first time and the parcel gets a real sortcode. Everything the network knows about this box is unchanged — same tracking number, same booking — it simply now has a barcode a camera can see.

steps.name: Chute assigned
steps.title: Chute 114 — airfreight export
steps.description: The sortcode resolves to one of 188 chutes. There is no chute for 'Japan' — there is a chute for the airside feeder that leaves at 03:40, and getting on that vehicle is the only decision being made here.

steps.name: Cage built
steps.title: Chute emptied into a cage and sealed
steps.description: Chutes hold about ninety parcels before they back up, so they are emptied into roll cages continuously through the shift. The cage is sealed against a departure time, not a parcel count — a half-empty cage still leaves at 03:40.

steps.name: Airside feeder
steps.title: Back at the top level: across the campus
steps.description: The hub and the cargo shed share a site, so the feeder never touches a public road — which matters, because the moment goods are destined for export they are handled under a different set of controls.

footer.text: **23 minutes idle** before this leg — the feeder waits for its slot, not for the parcel.

steps.name: ULD build
steps.title: Cages become aircraft containers
steps.description: Roll cages cannot go on a plane. Parcels are broken out and rebuilt into ULDs — aluminium containers shaped to the curve of the fuselage — against a load plan that balances the aircraft as much as it fills it.

footer.text: Cut-off for a long-haul freighter is **six hours** before departure, not one.

steps.name: Loaded and away
steps.title: Containers go up the loader
steps.description: Six ULDs go through the main-deck door on a scissor loader and are locked to the floor rails. The last scan on this side of the world is the container's, not the parcel's — the box itself is now invisible until it lands.

steps.name: Eleven hours
steps.title: The longest event in the journey
steps.description: Eleven hours in which nothing can be scanned, nothing can be re-routed and no question can be answered. It is a quarter of the total transit time and the only leg of the whole journey that cannot be improved by better operations.

footer.text: **11 h 00 airborne** — 26% of the total 42-hour journey, in one bar.

steps.name: Presented to border
steps.title: Wheels down, but not in the country yet
steps.description: The ULD is broken down in the arrival shed and the parcels are scanned back into existence. Legally none of them have entered Japan: they are in a bonded area, treated as outside the customs territory until the border says otherwise.

steps.name: Entry lodged
steps.title: Inside the border post: the paperwork got here first
steps.description: The carrier lodged an electronic declaration against the flight manifest before the aircraft even left. Pre-lodgement is the single reason most parcels clear in minutes rather than days — the border has had eleven hours to think about this box.

footer.text: This bar **overlaps the flight** — the declaration was cleared for processing while the parcel was still airborne.

steps.name: Document check
steps.title: The declaration is matched to the airway bill
steps.description: Commodity code, declared value, country of origin and consignee are checked against the airway bill. A wrong commodity code is by far the most common reason a low-value parcel gets stuck — the goods are fine, the four digits describing them are not.

steps.name: Risk scored
steps.title: The channel is chosen by a score, not a person
steps.description: Commodity, route, consignor history and declared value produce a risk score, and the score picks the channel. Nobody looks at the box to decide whether to look at the box.

steps.name: Green channel
steps.title: Most parcels never stop
steps.description: A dual-energy scanner colours the image by material density, so an operator can tell paper from metal from electronics without opening anything. Nine in ten parcels go straight from the scanner to duty assessment, in the time it takes to walk past the machine.

footer.text: **~90% green.** Scanning is cheap and exists purely to keep the number of boxes actually opened low.

steps.name: Flagged
steps.title: This one is not one of them
steps.description: The image shows a dense rectangular block the declaration does not obviously account for — in this case the interface's power supply. That is enough to move the parcel to the red channel and into a bonded cage to wait for an officer.

footer.text: **2–3% of parcels** are physically examined, and the selection is a score — not a lottery.

steps.name: Opened
steps.title: An officer opens the box
steps.description: The goods are checked against the declaration, photographed, and the box resealed with tamper tape. The result is recorded against the consignor, so a clean examination today lowers the score on their next hundred shipments.

footer.text: **1 h 24 m in the cage** — nearly all of it waiting for an officer, not being examined.

steps.name: Duty assessed
steps.title: Tariff and import tax on the landed cost
steps.description: Duty is charged on cost plus insurance plus freight, not on what the sender paid for the item — so the shipping cost is itself taxable. Import consumption tax is then applied on top of the duty-inclusive value.

steps.name: Released
steps.title: The bond is lifted
steps.description: Release is a status change in a database, and only now has the parcel legally entered the country. The box has not moved a metre — but everything downstream was waiting on this one flag.

footer.text: **2 h 48 m at the border** against a 15-minute green-channel norm — the exam cost most of it.

steps.name: Into the domestic network
steps.title: Back outside: handed to the partner carrier
steps.description: The origin carrier has no vans in Japan, so the parcel is handed to a domestic partner. It gets a second tracking number and a domestic sortcode; the two numbers are linked so the sender's tracking page keeps working.

footer.text: One parcel, **two tracking numbers**. The handover is as much a data join as a physical one.

steps.name: Overnight trunk
steps.title: One more hub, one more night
steps.description: The destination country runs the same hub-and-spoke shape as the origin, so the parcel spends another night on a trunk trailer being sorted with everything else going to the same city. Two national networks, the same physics.

steps.name: Round loaded
steps.title: Sorted to a round, then to a van
steps.description: The depot sorts to a round, not to an address — the order of stops within the round is decided later by the driver's handheld and re-decided all morning as traffic and failed deliveries change it.

footer.text: The final mile is roughly **half the cost** of the entire journey.

steps.name: Out for delivery
steps.title: The first message the recipient gets
steps.description: A single scan at the van bay triggers the only notification most people ever receive. Forty hours of network activity produce one text message, and everything before it was invisible.

data.text: Your parcel is out for delivery today, 61st stop

steps.name: Doorstep
steps.title: Stop 61 of 96
steps.description: The driver scans the barcode at the door, collects the import tax on a card reader and takes a photograph. That scan is the same kind of event as the very first one in Bristol — the network's whole life is barcodes and timestamps.

steps.name: Delivered
steps.title: 41 hours 45 minutes, 62 scan events
steps.description: Of the total journey, eleven hours were airborne, three were spent at the border and under an hour was spent actually being sorted. Nearly everything else was the parcel waiting for a vehicle that leaves on a timetable — which is what a parcel network really is: a set of departure times with boxes queued behind them.

footer.text: **41 h 45 m door to door**, of which about **50 minutes** was machine handling.
The scuffed label cost **31 minutes** — one no-read, one queue, one second pass.
